description:
Hello from Space Spark! We are a team of researchers and tech enthusiasts with deep interests in precision agriculture, climate-smart solutions, and bio-environmental systems. By taking on "Adapting Farms with NASA Data," we aim to empower agricultural communities to adapt to shifting climate patterns using real-time satellite insights.
We bring strong skills in scientific research, system architecture, Python, and project management. If you want a collaborative team that values both technical !
summary:
We developed CropTwin, a data-driven decision sandbox that helps farmers decide what to plant, when, and how to protect it before committing to a season. We use the NASA datasets provided on the Space Apps platform, including NASA POWER for solar radiation, temperature, and precipitation, and SMAP for soil moisture, and we augment them with our own local ground-truth weather data to calibrate and localize the signals.

The system computes a Crop Suitability Score for each crop and explains whether it is suitable, suitable with precautions, or not suitable-and why. If a crop is at risk, farmers test tangible rescue cards such as Pulse Irrigation, 50% Shading, Mulching, and Flood Irrigation. Each card is tied to a physics-based model (FAO Crop Coefficient, Water Balance, ET₀), so the system recalculates the Crop Stress Index and Health Bar in real time and shows a Control vs Treated comparison with an actionable prescription.

CropTwin addresses the challenge of adapting farms with NASA Earth observation data by combining NASA-provided datasets with local data to turn complex space data into explainable, testable, farm-level decisions. It is important because it reduces agricultural risk, saves water, and supports food security-empowering farmers to act before disasters strike.
details:
CropTwin is a web-based climate-risk decision simulator that answers the one question a farmer actually asks — "Is this crop viable here for the next two weeks, and what do I do if it isn't?" — instead of leaving them with scattered data.

The problem it closes: A farmer has data everywhere — local weather stations returning raw numbers, NASA POWER at 0.5° (~50 km), SMAP soil moisture at 9–36 km with 2–3 day latency, MODIS/VIIRS NDVI at 250–1000 m — but no decision layer that converts any of it into "plant this / don't plant this / do this now."

The pipeline works in six steps:

Step 1 — Data ingestion. We use NASA datasets from the Space Apps platform: NASA POWER (T2M, T2M_MAX/MIN, RH2M, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, PRECTOTCORR — 0.5°, daily), SMAP SPL4SMGP (surface and root-zone soil moisture, 9–36 km, 2–3 days), GPM-IMERG (precipitation, 0.1°, daily), MODIS/VIIRS (NDVI, LST — 250–1000 m, daily), ECOSTRESS (land-surface temperature and ET, ~70 m), and NLDAS/GLDAS (gridded temperature, precipitation, soil moisture and ET proxies for gap-filling) — combined with our own local ground-truth weather station reading temperature, humidity, pressure, light and soil moisture every minute.

Step 2 — Calibration / bias correction. NASA's macro-scale signal is corrected against our on-site sensors daily. Example from the Delta: NASA POWER Tmax = 38.9 °C, our station recorded 40.2 °C → a +1.3 °C offset is applied to the entire NASA series for that location, so the data reflects the farmer's exact field rather than a 50 km average.

Step 3 — Physics-based model. FAO-56 evapotranspiration (ETc = Kc × ET₀, with ET₀ derived via Hargreaves from NASA radiation and temperature), a daily soil-water balance (SM(t+1) = SM(t) + Irrigation + Rain − ETc − Drainage), and a Crop Suitability Score (CSS) from 0–100 built on five weighted, fully displayed components: temperature (0.30), water (0.25), radiation (0.20), heat/frost risk (0.15), soil (0.10).

Step 4 — Verdict with reasons. Suitable (CSS ≥ 70), Suitable with Precautions (50–69), or Not Suitable (< 50) — each with the exact causes listed: Heatwave, Water Deficit, Frost Risk, or Radiation Stress.

Step 5 — Interactive rescue cards. The farmer tests decisions using tangible cards read by an FSR sensor (Pulse Irrigation, 50% Shading, Mulching, Flood Irrigation). Every card is a model input, not an animation: Pulse Irrigation raises soil moisture (+6 mm/day), 50% Shading cuts ETc by ~30% and lowers heat and radiation stress, Mulching reduces the evaporation term in the water balance, and Flood Irrigation is rejected for high water use and salinity risk. A side-by-side Control vs Treated comparison shows the impact — the improvement is demonstrated, not claimed.

Step 6 — Prescription. The system outputs a concrete recommendation, e.g. "Run irrigation 3 minutes every 20 minutes with 50% shading for 5 days."

Worked example from our validation (Delta, wheat, heatwave forecast):

  • ET₀ = 0.0023 × 16.0 × (32.5 + 17.8) × √(41 − 24) = 7.6 mm/day
  • ETc = 1.15 × 7.6 = 8.8 mm/day (FAO-56, mid-season Kc)
  • Sub-scores: Temp 42, Water 32, Radiation 45, Heat/Frost 38, Soil 70
  • CSS = 0.30·42 + 0.25·32 + 0.20·45 + 0.15·38 + 0.10·70 = 42.3 → Not Suitable
  • After Pulse Irrigation + 50% Shading: sub-scores 58 / 78 / 72 / 62 / 72 → CSS = 67.8 → Suitable with Precautions
  • CSI: 0.72 → 0.31 · Health Bar: 28% → 69%

2. Benefits

  • Water savings — wasteful strategies are rejected by the model, not merely reported: up to ~40% lower seasonal water use versus flood irrigation in our scenarios.
  • Reduced risk — the farmer acts before the heatwave, not after the loss.
  • Explainability — every score comes with its reasons and its normalized weights displayed on screen; nothing is a black box.
  • Accessibility — the entire experience runs in any browser, with no installation and no app store.
  • Scalability — a new crop or region needs only a new FAO Kc profile and a local calibration point; no new hardware.
  • Repeatability — same input produces the same output every run, which makes the system auditable and testable.

3. Intended impact

Egypt draws ~97% of its irrigation water from the Nile, so a single wrong irrigation decision is a national water cost, not just a farm loss. CropTwin turns complex Earth observation data into a decision a farmer can act on today — supporting water conservation, climate adaptation, and food security. The intended impact is threefold: save water by rejecting wasteful strategies at the decision point, reduce risk by letting farmers test a season before betting on it, and support food security by making rotation and planting choices informed rather than intuitive. We state our claim honestly: we do not guarantee the harvest — we reduce the risk.

4. Tools, coding languages, hardware & software

Data: NASA POWER, SMAP (SPL4SMGP), GPM-IMERG, MODIS/VIIRS, ECOSTRESS, NLDAS/GLDAS, plus our own local ground-truth weather station.

Backend: Python / Flask — data ingestion, bias-correction calibration, the model engine (ET₀, water balance, CSS, CSI), and a REST API.

Frontend: React — a browser-based interface for location and crop selection, verdicts with reasons, rescue cards, the Control vs Treated comparison, and prescriptions. No mobile app is required; the entire experience is web-based.

Hardware: ESP32 microcontroller inside a custom acrylic micro-chamber, with DHT22 (temperature ±0.5 °C, humidity ±2–5%), BMP280 (pressure ±1 hPa), BH1750 (light, 1–65,535 lux), capacitive soil-moisture sensors (±3%), and an FSR card reader with on-screen button fallback. Communication is over WiFi/MQTT to the backend. Each card carries a distinct FSR weight signature — Pulse Irrigation 120 g, Shading 185 g, Mulching 240 g, Flood Irrigation 310 g.

Model references: FAO-56 (crop coefficients), NASA POWER documentation, SMAP SPL4SMGP product specification, GPM IMERG (NASA GES DISC).

5. How the project is creative

CropTwin's core innovation is closing the loop between space data and physical interaction. Existing tools are either software-only dashboards (AquaCrop, FieldView) or macro-scale satellite viewers — both report numbers and stop there. We built the missing decision layer: NASA data is calibrated against real local sensors, and the farmer physically places a rescue card on an FSR-powered arena, immediately watching a physics-based model recalculate stress, health and suitability, with a Control vs Treated comparison proving the change. The result is a repeatable, explainable "flight simulator" for farming — a farmer can test a decision before betting a season on it. Two further creative choices matter: the model rejects bad decisions (Flood Irrigation is refused for water use and salinity risk) rather than passively accepting any input; and the whole system is web-based and hardware-augmented, requiring no app installation while still grounding the simulation in real microclimate readings from the ESP32 chamber.

6. Factors the team considered

  • Data honesty. SMAP is 9–36 km with 2–3 day latency; it is not field-level or real-time. We state this openly rather than overclaiming, and explain how calibration and NLDAS gap-filling mitigate it.
  • Calibration over stacking. NASA macro-signals alone are insufficient for farm decisions, which is why local ground-truth data drives daily bias correction (the +1.3 °C Delta example).
  • Model transparency. All weights are normalized and displayed on screen, so any reviewer or farmer can audit a result.
  • Hardware reliability. Each card has a distinct FSR weight signature, with on-screen button fallback if the sensor fails, so the demo and the product never depend on a single point of failure.
  • Validation scope. We validated on three deliberately different scenarios — Delta/wheat (heat + moisture deficit), Aswan/maize (extreme heat), and Delta/spinach (moderate conditions) — to confirm the model does not simply default to "Not Suitable."
  • Stated limitations. The model is validated on scenario tests only with no field trials yet; FAO Kc values are reference values not locally calibrated; ET₀ uses simplified Hargreaves rather than full Penman-Monteith; and a single local station gives point-based rather than spatial bias correction. Each of these defines a concrete item on our validation roadmap, which begins with live crop bio-sensors for field calibration.
